topicDisplay: Paper 1 Language The Individual And Society
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The grammatical term 'syntax' refers to:
options: The rules governing how words combine into phrases, clauses and sentences
questions.explain: Syntax concerns the arrangement and combination of words into larger grammatical structures.

questions.q: An 'adjacency pair' in conversation analysis is:
options: Two words placed next to each other
A paired sequence of turns such as question and answer
Two clauses joined by a conjunction
questions.explain: Adjacency pairs are linked utterance turns where the first part conventionally expects a specific second, e.g. greeting/greeting.

questions.q: The 'holophrastic' stage of child language is so called because the child:
options: Uses a single word to express a whole idea or sentence
questions.explain: In the holophrastic (one-word) stage a single word such as 'milk' conveys a complete proposition or request.

questions.q: The 'interactional' function in Halliday's framework is used by children to:
options: Build and maintain relationships with others
questions.explain: The interactional function ('love you') develops and sustains social relationships between the child and others.

questions.q: Which theorist proposed an innate 'Language Acquisition Device' (LAD)?
questions.explain: Chomsky's nativist theory argues children possess an innate LAD enabling rapid grammar acquisition from limited input.

questions.q: A child who calls all four-legged animals 'dog' is displaying:
questions.explain: Over-extension is applying a word too broadly to include items beyond its conventional meaning.

questions.q: In Accommodation Theory, 'divergence' refers to:
options: Emphasising the differences between one's speech and another's
questions.explain: Divergence is accentuating differences in speech, often to assert identity or distance.

questions.q: The two-word stage is significant because it marks the first appearance of:
questions.explain: At the two-word stage children begin combining words in consistent order, showing early grammatical/syntactic awareness.

questions.q: When a child says 'goed' instead of 'went', this is best described as:
options: Over-generalisation of a grammatical rule (a virtuous error)
questions.explain: 'Goed' shows over-generalisation of the regular past-tense rule to an irregular verb, evidence the child is applying rules rather than imitating.

questions.q: Standard English is best understood as:
options: A prestige dialect used in formal and written contexts, independent of accent
A regional accent of the south-east
questions.explain: Standard English is a prestige dialect of grammar and vocabulary that can be spoken in any accent.

questions.q: A 'sociolect' is best defined as a variety of language associated with:
options: A particular social group or class
questions.explain: A sociolect is a variety linked to a social group, such as a class or community.

questions.q: Labov's New York findings linked higher rates of post-vocalic /r/ pronunciation with:
options: Higher social status and overt prestige
questions.explain: More /r/ pronunciation correlated with higher social status, reflecting the overt prestige of that form.

questions.q: Peter Trudgill linked the use of standard forms more strongly with which group in his Norwich study?
questions.explain: Trudgill found women tended to use more standard forms and to over-report them, oriented to overt prestige.

questions.q: 'Dialect levelling' refers to the process by which:
options: Regional differences reduce and varieties become more similar
Dialects become more distinct over time
questions.explain: Dialect levelling is the reduction of differences between dialects, often through increased mobility and contact.

questions.q: An 'occupational variety' such as legal or medical language is often called:
options: A jargon or register tied to a profession
questions.explain: Occupational varieties involve specialised jargon and registers shared by members of a profession.

questions.q: Piaget's theory links language development to:
options: The child's underlying cognitive development and stages of thought
questions.explain: Piaget argued language reflects and depends on cognitive maturation; children can only express concepts they have cognitively developed.

questions.q: Received Pronunciation (RP) is best classified as:
questions.explain: RP is an accent, traditionally prestigious and not tied to any one region, not a full dialect.

questions.q: Cohesion in a text is achieved by devices such as:
options: Pronoun reference, conjunctions and lexical repetition
questions.explain: Cohesion is created through grammatical and lexical ties such as anaphoric reference, connectives and repetition that bind a text together.

questions.q: In linguistic analysis, the term 'graphology' refers to the study of which aspect of a text?
options: The visual and presentational features such as layout, font and colour
The personality of the writer revealed by handwriting
The sounds and their physical articulation
questions.explain: In language study graphology denotes the visual aspects of a text (typography, layout, images), not the popular pseudoscience of handwriting analysis.

questions.q: In phonological development, voiced sounds and front consonants like /p/, /b/, /m/ tend to be acquired:
questions.explain: Bilabial and other front consonants such as /p/, /b/, /m/ are typically among the earliest sounds children produce.

questions.q: Howard Giles's 'matched-guise' technique is used to study:
options: Listeners' attitudes towards accents and varieties
questions.explain: The matched-guise technique reveals attitudes by having one speaker read passages in different guises.

questions.q: A child who uses the word 'cup' only for their own special cup and no other cups is showing:
questions.explain: Under-extension restricts a word's meaning to fewer referents than the adult use allows.

questions.q: 'Child-directed speech' (CDS), formerly called motherese, is typically characterised by:
options: Complex subordinate clauses and rapid speech
Higher pitch, exaggerated intonation, repetition and simplified vocabulary
Use of jargon and technical terms
questions.explain: CDS features raised pitch, slower tempo, repetition and simplified syntax, thought to support acquisition.

questions.q: The 'cooing' stage typically occurs at approximately:
questions.explain: Cooing, comprising open vowel-like sounds, emerges from around 6-8 weeks, before babbling begins.

questions.q: Multicultural London English (MLE) is best described as:
options: An emerging ethnolect arising from diverse urban contact
A historical form of Old English
A regional dialect of the North
questions.explain: MLE is a contact variety that emerged in multi-ethnic, multilingual areas of London.

questions.q: 'Implicature' is best described as:
options: The grammatical subject of a clause
What is directly and explicitly stated
Meaning that is implied or inferred beyond the literal words
questions.explain: Implicature, central to Gricean pragmatics, is the additional meaning a hearer infers from an utterance in context.

questions.q: Halliday's taxonomy of language functions includes the 'instrumental' function, which is used to:
questions.explain: In Halliday's model the instrumental function expresses needs ('want milk'), while the regulatory function controls others' behaviour.

questions.q: Which is the most accurate description of 'phonology' as opposed to 'phonetics'?
options: Phonology studies the physical production of speech sounds; phonetics studies sound systems
Phonology studies how sounds function and pattern in a language; phonetics studies the physical properties of sounds
questions.explain: Phonetics deals with the physical articulation/acoustics of speech sounds, while phonology studies how sounds function within a particular language system.

questions.q: In analysing mode, electronic communication such as instant messaging is often described as:
options: Purely written with no spoken features
Occupying a position on a continuum, blending spoken and written features
questions.explain: Electronically mediated communication blends speech-like immediacy with written form, sitting between the spoken and written ends of a mode continuum.

questions.q: In the post-telegraphic stage, a notable development is the appearance of:
options: Function words, inflections and more complex, grammatically complete structures
questions.explain: Post-telegraphic speech increasingly includes determiners, auxiliaries, inflections and complex/compound sentences toward adult grammar.
